questions.question: Describe how the justice system works from a crime to a court decision.
questions.expected_answer: When a crime is reported, the police investigate, collect evidence and may arrest a suspect. A prosecutor from the National Prosecuting Authority decides whether to charge the person and presents the case for the state. The accused has a right to a lawyer, provided free by Legal Aid in many cases. A magistrate or judge listens to both sides, decides whether the accused is guilty and, if so, decides the sentence. Courts range from magistrates' courts to high courts, the Supreme Court of Appeal and the Constitutional Court.

questions.question: Explain what equality before the law and the right to a fair trial mean.
questions.expected_answer: Equality before the law means the law treats every person the same, whatever their wealth, power, race, gender, religion or language, as section 9 of the Bill of Rights says. A fair trial means an accused person is presumed innocent until the state proves guilt, is told the charges, may remain silent, has a lawyer, has a trial within a reasonable time and may appeal. Courts must be independent and impartial.

questions.question: Why is the Constitutional Court important for democracy?
questions.expected_answer: It is the highest court and protects the Constitution and Bill of Rights. It can declare laws passed by Parliament or actions of the government unconstitutional and invalid, which keeps the other branches within their limits and protects people's rights. For example, in 1995 it abolished the death penalty because it went against the rights to life and dignity. It stands on Constitution Hill, a former prison, as a symbol of justice replacing injustice.
